A close reading for the week

“the pathway from slavery to freedom”

Frederick Douglass · Chapter VI

When Hugh Auld forbids his wife to teach Douglass to read, he means to preserve control. His prohibition gives Douglass an explanation of that control instead, and a purpose.

These words sank deep into my heart,1 stirred up sentiments within that lay slumbering, and called into existence an entirely new train of thought.

It was a new and special revelation,2 explaining dark and mysterious things, with which my youthful understanding had struggled, but struggled in vain. I now understood what had been to me a most perplexing difficulty—to wit, the white man’s power to enslave the black man.

  1. 1

    Words enter and awaken

    ‘Sank’, ‘stirred’ and ‘slumbering’ make thought a movement inside the body. Auld’s words tell Douglass something he was already close to understanding, and give it a shape.

  2. 2

    A secular revelation

    “Revelation” gives the discovery the force of disclosed truth. What he sees is why reading has been forbidden to him.
